title: Olney Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Olney Springs wells have a 40-foot median depth, but costs vary with construction, pumps, trenching and electrical work.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around Olney Springs, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records around Olney Springs show a shallow plains-water setting, but the records also contain a wide range of outcomes. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 31 to 50 feet. That is useful for an initial budget, not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Most recorded wells are in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a smaller number in alluvial units. Before buying near Crowley, Fowler, or the surrounding Crowley County farmland, review nearby well permits, confirm the intended use, and have a driller evaluate access, casing, grout, pump sizing, and septic separation.

sections.heading: Shallow wells are typical around Olney Springs
sections.html:
The local depth record is unusually concentrated near the surface. 96% of the wells are under 100 feet, while the middle half of reported depths is only 31 to 50 feet. The 90th percentile is 76 feet, so a contractor estimating a routine domestic well may start with a shallow drilling allowance.

That does not eliminate surprises. The deepest well in the record is 1,550 feet, and a small share reaches the 100 to 300-foot range or beyond. The ground is described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Local changes in sand, gravel, clay, cemented layers, or fractured rock can change both drilling time and the final casing and grout design.

sections.heading: Reported well yields are strong, but the sample is limited
sections.html:
Only 44 wells report a pump yield, so treat the yield statistics as a guide rather than a promise for every parcel. In that reporting group, the median is 225 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15 to 600 gallons per minute. 77% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 18% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 5% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That pattern is favorable for many uses, but a high reported yield may reflect irrigation or stock wells rather than a household well. Ask for the well use, pump test details, and permit conditions. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, and a strong well still needs properly sized pump, pressure tank, storage, and electrical service.

sections.heading: Water levels near Olney Springs appear relatively shallow
sections.html:
Only 16 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth record. Within those reports, the median depth to water is 22 feet, and the middle half is 13 to 28 feet. For construction planning, that suggests many wells may encounter water well above their total drilled depth.

The permit counts by decade do not establish a water-table trend. They show activity from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025, but they do not provide comparable water-level readings for each decade. Do not assume the water table is rising or falling from permit counts alone. A driller can check nearby logs and measure an existing well where access is available.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Olney Springs and the nearby plains have a long well-permit history. Records include 82 permits from the 1950s, 55 from the 1960s, 31 from the 1970s, and 29 from the 1980s. Later records include 66 in the 1990s, 64 in the 2000s, 48 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s.

The most active names in these records are Crandall, H A with 40 wells, Broce Drilling (Broce, Frank R.) with 31, and Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl) with 23. These are historical permit records, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and who will handle the permit, testing, pump installation, and completion report.

sections.heading: A median-depth well has a manageable starting budget
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35 to $55 per foot for drilling in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 40-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,400 to $2,200. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $7,400 to $14,200.

Use that range for early planning, not as a fixed bid. Access for the rig, casing and grout requirements, pump depth, trench length, difficult layers, water testing, and power connection can move the price. A lot near Crowley or Fowler may have a different access and trenching problem than a parcel with an established driveway. Get the drilling and completion items separated in writing before comparing bids.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and low-yield risk
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features in that mapped set. Those records do not prove contamination at a specific home, but they are a reason to identify the sites, check the proposed lot’s distance and drainage relationship, and order water testing after completion.

Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported sample, yet the sample is limited and dry holes remain possible. Confirm the permit’s allowed use, test for bacteria and relevant local contaminants, and leave room for a compliant septic system, replacement area, access, and building setbacks. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses.

sections.heading: Buy the lot after reviewing its neighbors and permit
sections.html:
For a purchase, start with the Colorado DWR permit record and inspect wells on adjoining or nearby parcels. Compare total depth, aquifer description, use, yield, static water level, casing, and completion notes rather than relying on one unusually productive well. Nearby places in the record area include Crowley and Fowler, with Manzanola also close enough to provide broader local context.

For a new build, ask a licensed driller to walk the access route and proposed well location before closing. Confirm that the well can serve the planned household use, that the septic layout works with the well location, and that electric service can reach the pump equipment. If the property will need irrigation, livestock water, or additional supply, address those uses with the water-rights and permit review instead of assuming a domestic well covers them.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Olney Springs, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Olney Springs is 40 feet. The middle half of wells is 31 to 50 feet, and 96% are under 100 feet. The record also includes a deepest well of 1,550 feet, so a nearby permit is more useful than a countywide assumption when budgeting for a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Olney Springs?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,400 to $2,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $7,400 to $14,200. Access, casing, grout, pump depth, trench length, and difficult ground can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Olney Springs?
faq.a: Yield data is limited to 44 wells, but the reported median is 225 gallons per minute and the middle half is 15 to 600 gallons per minute. Seventy-seven percent of those reported yields exceed 15 gallons per minute. Because many records may represent irrigation or stock uses, ask for the specific well’s pump test and permitted use before relying on the number.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Olney Springs?
faq.a: The permit map includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That does not establish contamination on a particular property, but it supports testing a new or transferred well for bacteria and relevant contaminants. Review nearby environmental sites, drainage, septic history, and the well’s construction record before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Olney Springs?
faq.a: The available records do not show a reliable decade-by-decade water-level trend. Only 16 wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 22 feet, with the middle half from 13 to 28 feet. Permit counts through the newest permit year, 2025, cannot show whether the water table is rising or falling. A local measurement and nearby well logs are better evidence.
